title: much, many, little, few, a lot, plenty
subtitle: much / many / little / few / a lot of / plenty of
summary: Choose much, many, little, few, a lot of or plenty of according to the noun and the sentence type, and tell the difference between little/few and a little/a few.

lesson.heading: Which words go with which nouns?
rows: much luck, much time, little energy, little money
many friends, many people, few children, few cars
a lot of / lots of / plenty of
a lot of luck, lots of time, plenty of money, a lot of friends, lots of people, plenty of ideas

lesson.heading: plenty = more than enough
lesson.text: **Plenty of** means more than enough. You can also say **plenty to** + verb.

examples.text: There's no need to hurry. We've got **plenty of** time.
There's **plenty to** do in this town.

left.label: much - questions and negatives
left.text: much is unusual in positive sentences, especially in spoken English
examples: We spent **too much** money. (too much / so much / as much are fine in positive sentences)

lesson.heading: many and a lot of
lesson.text: We use **many** and **a lot of** in all kinds of sentences - positive, negative and questions. Note that we say **many years / many weeks / many days**.

examples.text: **Many** people drive too fast. or **A lot of** people drive too fast.
Do you know **many** people? or Do you know **a lot of** people?
There aren't **many** tourists here. or There aren't **a lot of** tourists here.

lesson.heading: little = not much, few = not many
lesson.text: **little** and **few** have a negative idea: less than you want or expect. We often say **very little** and **very few**.

examples.text: Gary is very busy with his job. He has **little** time for other things.
examples.note: = not much time, less time than he would like

examples.text: Vicky doesn't like living in London. She has **few** friends there.
examples.note: = not many friends, not as many as she would like

examples.text: Gary has **very little** time for other things.
Vicky has **very few** friends in London.

lesson.heading: a little = some, a few = some
lesson.text: **a little** = some, a small amount. **a few** = some, a small number. These have a positive idea: not a lot, but enough.

examples.text: Let's go and have coffee. We have **a little** time before the train leaves.
examples.note: = some time, enough time to have a coffee
so we can talk a bit

examples.text: I enjoy my life here. I have **a few** friends and we meet quite often.
examples.note: = not many, but enough to have a good time

examples.text: 'When was the last time you saw Clare?' '**A few** days ago.'

lesson.heading: little / few or a little / a few?

left.label: little / few (negative: not much, not many)
examples: He spoke **little** English, so it was difficult to communicate with him.

right.label: a little / a few (positive: some)
examples: He spoke **a little** English, so we were able to communicate with him.
Things are not going so well for her. She has **a few** problems.

lesson.note: We say only a little (not only little) and only a few (not only few): Hurry! We only have a little time. The village was small. There were only a few houses.

lesson.text: In positive statements prefer a lot of: We spent a lot of money, not ~~We spent much money~~.

exercises.statement: Be quick. We don't have much time.
exercises.explanation: Correct. much is natural in negative sentences and questions.

exercises.statement: It cost much to repair the car.
exercises.explanation: It cost a lot to repair the car. much is unusual in positive sentences.

exercises.prompt: You have ___ luggage. Let me help you.
exercises.explanation: A positive sentence, so a lot of (not much). luggage is uncountable, so many is impossible.

exercises.prompt: Which nouns go with much / little and which with many / few?
Match the beginnings with the endings that use plenty of ... or plenty to ...

pairs.right: she still has plenty to learn.

pairs.left: It's an interesting town to visit.
I'm sure we'll find somewhere to stay.

exercises.prompt: Anna is very busy these days. She has ___ free time.
exercises.explanation: free time is uncountable and the idea is negative (not much), so little.

exercises.prompt: Did you take ___ pictures at the wedding?
exercises.explanation: pictures is plural and this is a question, so many.

exercises.statement: I don't know much people in this town.
exercises.explanation: I don't know many people (or a lot of people) in this town. people is plural, so many, not much.

exercises.prompt: It was the middle of the night, so there was ___.
exercises.explanation: little = not much, a negative idea: there was hardly any traffic. traffic is uncountable, so few is impossible.
We say only a few (not only few); words is plural, so a few, not a little.

exercises.prompt: Listen carefully. I'm going to give you ___ advice.
exercises.explanation: a little = some, a small amount; advice is uncountable.

exercises.prompt: I don't think Amy would be a good teacher. She has ___ patience.
exercises.explanation: little = not much, a negative idea: she doesn't have enough patience.
